items.title: Mcbee interviewed by Monk Rowe, 2020
items.q: But the very next year I joined the Charles Lloyd Quartet.

ctx.x: Well my question is, moving from placing quarter notes and swing and playing on top of the beat, this was a totally different task for you it seems like, playing a bass line repetitively in some cases basically the similar thing all the way through, while other players did their explorations. Like you were the anchor. And I wonder if you enjoyed that role, for sometimes the songs could go on for eight or nine minutes. How do you keep your concentration?

You don’t concentrate, you just feel it. Something like that, by that I mean it’s just a vibe. You are now as a bassist, you are now being rather responsible to maintain the bass line that would support all that is happening beyond you melodically, harmonically, etcetera, etcetera. It was something, quite frankly, that I was already sort of familiar with. Number one my second group — my first group that I performed with in New York City was with Jackie McLean. He trained Bobby Hutcherson, Charles Tolliver, and…
This is sort of a personal question, do you feel you are a spiritual man? Does faith play a significant role in your life?

items.title: Mcbee interviewed by Monk Rowe, 2020
items.q: By now I’m playing literally around the world with Keith Jarrett, Jack DeJohnette, and Charles Lloyd. And we are having a great time.

ctx.x: Beautiful. Just to wrap up, an acquaintance knew I was going to be talking to you and he said, “Oh he’s played with everyone. I’m curious if he ever recorded with Miles Davis?”

No. I didn’t record with Miles Davis, but I had an episode with Miles Davis. Herbie Hancock called me — well what’s that, my first recording we discussed before, with Grachan Moncur featuring Herbie Hancock, Wayne Shorter and Tony Williams. This is how I met Herbie and those guys. And so apparently I was rather impressive with my dynamic. Herbie called me and says, “Miles would like you to do a performance with him.” So I said, “Yeah, okay.” And by now, I mean that was like a couple of years later. By now I’m…

mean playing with Jack and Keith were just all I was about. But on 77th Street on the third floor of Miles’ brownstone we had gone through all the tunes, the music was like that — right? And no Miles Davis. Right? So at the conclusion of the rehearsal, the last tune in the Key of C there was Herbie and Wayne were at the piano discussing the voicing of a G something chord, a G 7 chord. And they couldn’t find it. All of a sudden burst through the door was Miles Davis. He went over to the piano and he said…
